screens.title: Process Management and Scheduling
screens.narratorSegment: Processes are simply instances of running programs. In this lesson you will learn to observe what is running, make safe decisions when a process misbehaves, and automate routine maintenance so the system stays reliable. We'll use the core tools that administrators rely on: ps for snapshots, top and htop for live views, kill for signalling processes, nice and renice to tune priority, and cron and at to schedule recurring or one-time jobs. You will also see how parent and child process relationships matter when tracking PIDs, and why graceful termination is usually preferred over forceful kills. I'll show concrete commands you can run, highlight common mistakes—like relying on relative paths in cron—and give practical examples such as creating a daily cleanup script and scheduling it with crontab. By the end you'll understand not just the commands but why each tool matters for system responsiveness and predictable automation. Think about a time when a single runaway job slowed a server; these techniques are exactly what you would use to diagnose and fix it safely.

screens.title: What is a Process? PID and PPID
screens.narratorSegment: A process is simply an instance of a running program. Every process receives a unique process identifier, the PID, which the kernel uses to manage it. Processes often have parent-child relationships: the PPID field shows the parent's PID and reveals which process launched a child. For example, your interactive shell is typically the parent of commands you run. This parent-child relationship forms a process tree and matters for clean shutdowns and for understanding ownership and signal propagation. If a parent exits, the child may be adopted by the init process. In practical terms, when you want to trace why a background job is running, check PPID to find the originating shell or service. A common misconception is to treat PID as permanent; PIDs are reused over time, so relying on an old PID without re-checking can target the wrong process. To practice, use ps aux or ps -ef: ps aux shows user, PID, C P U and memory usage, and command, while ps -ef includes UID, PID, PPID, and a tree-like full format. Always re-check a PID immediately before sending signals. To reinforce this, try creating a short background job, note its PID, and then inspect its PPID to confirm the parent that launched it.

keyIdea.title: PID vs PPID
keyIdea.text: PID uniquely identifies a running process; PPID identifies the parent that launched it. PIDs can be reused, so verify before acting.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Process Identity
Definition and relationship

A process is an executing program instance. PID is its unique identifier while PPID points to the parent process. PIDs are allocated by the kernel and may be reused after a process exits.

  • Why PPID matters: trace who started the job, find shells or supervisors responsible for processes.
  • Lifecycle: parent can spawn children; orphaned children are adopted by the init process.
  • Practical tip: always re-check a PID right before sending a signal because PIDs can be reassigned.
Key Takeaway

PID locates a process now; PPID links it to its launcher. Use both for safe administration.

Quick commands
Use these ps variants to inspect processes. The code panel shows readable examples to try in a shell.
ps aux    # BSD style: shows all users, PID, CPU, MEM, TTY, STAT, START, COMMAND
ps -ef    # SysV style: shows UID, PID, PPID, C, STIME, TTY, TIME, CMD
Example scenario
Start a background task, note its PID, then run ps -ef and confirm PPID matches your shell PID. If not, investigate the parent process to see who launched it.

screens.title: Using top and htop for real-time monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Real-time monitoring shows how resources are used now. top is available on nearly every Linux system and provides a continuously-updating snapshot of C P U, memory, tasks, and the processes consuming them. It sorts by C P U by default, so heavy compute jobs float to the top. htop is an enhanced alternative with color, easier navigation, and built-in shortcuts to kill processes or renice them. For troubleshooting, start top and watch the C P U column and load averages to judge system health. When you see a process consuming most C P U, note its PID and consider whether it should be limited, reniced, or terminated. A common mistake is to rely solely on instantaneous spikes; look for sustained high usage before deciding to kill a process. Also check memory usage and swap activity — high swap indicates memory pressure and can make a system sluggish. Practice: run a harmless C P U-heavy background job and watch it appear in top or htop, record its PID, then practice lowering its priority with renice or stopping it safely. These tools are about observation first and intervention second.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Real-time Monitoring
top and htop
Continuous resource monitoring for CPU, memory, and processes
Core view and interpretation
  • top provides system summary: uptime, load averages, tasks, CPU states, memory usage.
  • Sort by CPU to find compute-heavy processes; look at the RES and %MEM columns for memory impact.
  • htop adds color, scrolling, and keyboard shortcuts to quickly locate and act on processes.
  • Watch for sustained high CPU or swap use before taking disruptive action.
Common mistake

Reacting to a single spike. Confirm the pattern before killing services used by others.

Try these commands
top    # live system monitor, press q to exit
# If installed:
htop   # interactive, colorized monitor with easy kill/renice
Example exercise
Start a harmless CPU loop in the background, open top, find the process by CPU percent and PID, then practice lowering its priority or sending a termination signal if needed.

screens.title: Signals and the kill command
screens.narratorSegment: Signals are the mechanism by which the kernel or other processes communicate with a running process. The kill command sends a signal to a process identified by PID. The usual sequence is to request graceful termination with SIGTERM, which allows the program to catch the signal and clean up resources. If SIGTERM fails because the process is stuck or unresponsive, SIGKILL forces immediate termination and cannot be caught by the process. Use SIGKILL carefully, because it prevents cleanup and can leave temporary files or databases in an inconsistent state. Another useful signal is SIGHUP, which many daemons interpret as a request to reload their configuration without a full restart. Common tools include killall and pkill, which target processes by name or pattern; these are convenient but risk affecting multiple processes unexpectedly. A safe workflow is: locate PID with ps or top, run kill PID, check whether the process exits, and only then escalate to kill -9 PID if necessary. Always verify the process you are targeting is the one you intend, and consider service-specific management tools for daemons where available.

keyIdea.title: Signal strategy
keyIdea.text: Send a graceful SIGTERM first. Use SIGKILL only as a last resort. Verify PIDs and prefer targeted signals over name-based broad kills.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Signals & kill
Common signals and meaning
  • SIGTERM (15): request graceful shutdown; process can clean up.
  • SIGKILL (9): immediate termination; cannot be trapped by the process.
  • SIGHUP (1): usually signals a daemon to reload configuration without restarting.
Mistake to avoid

Using kill -9 as the first action. It prevents cleanup and can cause data inconsistency.

Command examples
kill 12345        # send SIGTERM (default)
kill -9 12345     # send SIGKILL (forceful)
kill -1 12345     # send SIGHUP to request config reload
Name-based tools
killall stops processes by exact name; pkill matches patterns. Use them carefully because they can affect multiple instances.

screens.title: Foreground, background, and job control
screens.narratorSegment: Job control is how you move commands between foreground and background and resume them when needed. When you append an ampersand to a command, the shell starts it in the background so you keep the prompt. Commands run in the foreground block the shell until they finish. You can suspend a foreground process and send it to the background, or bring background jobs back to the foreground. These controls matter during interactive sessions and for managing tasks without opening new terminals. A common misconception is that background jobs consume no resources; they still use C P U and memory but allow the shell to accept new input. Use job control for short, interactive tasks; for persistent background work prefer system services or scheduled jobs. In practice, start a safe C P U-intensive command in the background, note the job number or PID, use ps or top to monitor it, then use fg or kill if you need to interact with or stop it. Learning to manage jobs reduces the temptation to reboot or disrupt other users when a process blocks your terminal.

keyIdea.text: Use & to background a job, fg to resume, and shell job management for interactive workflows. Background jobs still consume resources.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Foreground & Background
Interactive job controls
  • Append & to run a command in the background and return to the prompt immediately.
  • Use jobs to list shell job numbers, fg to bring a job to the foreground, and bg to resume a suspended job in the background.
  • Background jobs still use CPU and memory; monitor them with ps or top.
Pro tip

For long-running background work, consider using system services or cron to avoid tying jobs to an interactive shell.

Commands & scenario
myjob &        # start in background
jobs            # list shell jobs
fg %1           # bring job number 1 to foreground
bg %1           # resume job 1 in background
Example
Start a harmless loop in background, observe it in top, then pause it and bring it to foreground to inspect its output. Use kill only if you must terminate it.

screens.title: nice and renice — adjusting process priority
screens.narratorSegment: nice and renice change a process's scheduling priority, telling the kernel how politely that process should request C P U time. The nice value ranges from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). When you start a new process with nice, you set its initial niceness; renice changes niceness of an existing process by PID. For example, starting a long-running script with a positive nice value makes it yield C P U to interactive users, keeping the system responsive. Conversely, negative nice values increase priority and usually require administrative privileges. A common misconception is that nice prevents a process from using C P U at all; in fact it only adjusts relative priority — a low priority process still runs when the C P U is available. Practical use cases include lowering priority for background backups or re-prioritizing a heavy job without killing it. Remember to check current priority and test the effect under load. Use renice when you need to adjust a running job identified via ps or top, rather than restarting it with a new nice value. nice and renice — adjusting process priority means use nice to start with a modified priority and renice to adjust an active process. favor positive nice values for background tasks to protect interactivity.. In practical terms, lower or raise cpu priority to balance system usage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use nice to start with a modified priority and renice to adjust an active process. Favor positive nice values for background tasks to protect interactivity.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › nice / renice
How niceness works
  • Niceness is a relative scheduling priority from -20 to 19.
  • Higher numeric niceness means lower priority and more yielding to others.
  • Only privileged users can request negative niceness (higher priority).
Key Takeaway

Adjust priority to protect interactive tasks; renice avoids restarting long processes.

Commands & examples
nice -n 10 ./long_task.sh    # start with lower priority
sudo renice -n -5 -p 12345     # raise priority of PID 12345
Scenario
You have a nightly backup job blocking interactive users during the day. Start it with a niceness of +10 so it runs only when the CPU is available, or renice it down during work hours if needed.

screens.title: cron and crontab — scheduling recurring tasks
screens.narratorSegment: cron runs scheduled commands or scripts at specific times and intervals. Each user has a crontab; the system also includes global crontabs and cron. d directories. Crontab entries follow five time fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week, followed by the command. A frequent mistake is using relative paths or assuming the interactive environment: cron runs with a minimal PATH and different environment variables. Always use absolute paths to commands and files, ensure scripts are executable, and redirect output to a logfile for debugging. For example, to run a cleanup script daily at 2:30 AM, add the line with explicit home path to crontab. Edit your personal crontab with crontab -e and verify entries with crontab -l. For troubleshooting, check that the cron daemon is running, confirm file permissions, and examine redirected logs. Use cron for recurring maintenance tasks like backups and cleanup, and remember the security implications: cron jobs run with the file owner's permissions, so validate scripts before scheduling them. This prevents accidental privilege escalation or sensitive data exposure. cron and crontab — scheduling recurring tasks means use absolute paths, make scripts executable, redirect output to logs, and verify crontab entries with crontab -l to ensure reliability.. In practical terms, write reliable crontab entries and avoid common pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: cron best practices
keyIdea.text: Use absolute paths, make scripts executable, redirect output to logs, and verify crontab entries with crontab -l to ensure reliability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › cron / crontab
Syntax and rules

Crontab lines have five time fields followed by the command. Use crontab -e to edit your user crontab and crontab -l to list it. Cron runs with a reduced environment, so include absolute paths and environment setup in scripts.

  • Fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week.
  • Use absolute paths for commands and files to avoid PATH issues.
  • Redirect stdout and stderr to logs to debug cron jobs.
Common pitfalls

Relative paths, missing execute permissions, and expecting interactive environment variables.

Example crontab entry
# run daily cleanup at 2:30 AM
30 2 * * * /home/youruser/cleanup.sh >> /home/youruser/cleanup.log 2>&1
Checklist before scheduling
  • Make script executable with chmod +x.
  • Use full paths for every command inside the script.
  • Redirect output to a log to capture failures.

screens.title: Common cron mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Many cron failures stem from the way cron executes jobs. Cron runs with a minimal PATH and without your interactive shell's environment, so commands that work in your terminal may fail in cron. The most common fix is to use absolute paths for every binary and file referenced. Also ensure the script is executable and has correct ownership. Another frequent issue is unhandled output: cron will mail stdout and stderr to the job owner by default. If you don't want that, redirect both streams to a logfile or to null. Syntax errors in crontab lines silently prevent jobs from running, so verify entries and, if unsure, use a crontab generator. Check that the cron daemon is running if jobs never execute. Finally, consider security: cron jobs run with the crontab owner's permissions. Avoid scheduling jobs that expose secrets or run with elevated privileges unless absolutely necessary. When in doubt, test commands interactively with the same environment variables and absolute paths you plan to put in cron to ensure they behave as expected. Common cron mistakes and how to avoid them means use absolute paths, set execute permissions, redirect output, verify syntax, and respect the security context of cron jobs.. In practical terms, paths, permissions, environment, and output handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. narration.text: Many cron failures stem from the way cron executes jobs. Cron runs with a minimal PATH and without your interactive shell's environment, so commands that work in your terminal may fail in cron. The most common fix is to use absolute paths for every binary and file referenced. Also ensure the script is executable and has correct ownership. Another frequent issue is unhandled output: cron will mail stdout and stderr to the job owner by default. If you don't want that, redirect both streams to a logfile or to null. Syntax errors in crontab lines silently prevent jobs from running, so verify entries and, if unsure, use a crontab generator. Check that the cron daemon is running if jobs never execute. Finally, consider security: cron jobs run with the crontab owner's permissions. Avoid scheduling jobs that expose secrets or run with elevated privileges unless absolutely necessary. When in doubt, test commands interactively with the same environment variables and absolute paths you plan to put in cron to ensure they behave as expected. Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › cron pitfalls
Checklist of common issues
  • Incorrect PATH: use absolute binary paths.
  • Permissions: ensure scripts are executable.
  • Environment: set needed variables inside scripts.
  • Output: redirect stdout and stderr to logs.
  • Syntax: validate crontab lines to avoid silent failures.
Example log redirection
0 3 * * * /home/you/cleanup.sh >> /var/log/cleanup.log 2>&1
Debug strategy
Run the script manually using the same environment and absolute paths before adding it to crontab. Check crontab -l for correct syntax and confirm the cron daemon is active.

screens.title: Using at for single future execution
screens.narratorSegment: The at utility schedules commands to run once at a specified future time. It's useful for one-off jobs like running a cleanup tonight or a one-time script at a particular hour. To create a job, invoke at with a time specification, type the commands, and end the input with end-of-file. You can view pending at jobs with atq and remove them with atrm using the job number. Because at jobs run in a batch environment, they share the same pitfalls as cron: minimal PATH and environment, so use absolute paths and ensure executable permissions. A common misuse is to schedule interactive commands that require a terminal. at runs in the background without interactive input, so only schedule non-interactive commands. In practice, at is excellent for ad-hoc administrative tasks that don't belong in crontab. Remember to verify the at daemon or service is enabled on your distribution; without it, commands won't run. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › at
How at works
  • Use at followed by a time spec to queue commands for one-time execution.
  • Type commands interactively and finish with end-of-file to schedule them.
  • Manage jobs with atq to list and atrm to remove.
Use case

Schedule a one-time cleanup or maintenance script to run when fewer users are active.

Example session
at 23:00 tomorrow
# at> /usr/local/bin/cleanup_temp_files.sh
# at>  (Ctrl+D)

atq   # list pending at jobs
atrm 2 # remove job number 2
Caveat
at jobs are non-interactive. If a task requires user input, schedule a wrapper script that sets environment and runs unattended commands instead.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: identify, terminate, and schedule cleanup
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through the hands-on scenario step by step so you can reproduce it in your lab. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Lab Walkthrough
Step-by-step commands (do not run on production)
# 1. Start a harmless CPU loop in background
yes > /dev/null &

# 2. Monitor processes
top    # or htop if installed
ps -ef | grep yes

# 3. Attempt graceful termination
kill <PID_OF_YES>
# if it doesn't stop:
kill -9 <PID_OF_YES>

# 4. Create cleanup script
# in ~/cleanup.sh
# make executable: chmod +x ~/cleanup.sh

# 5. Schedule daily in crontab
crontab -e
# add: 0 3 * * * /home/youruser/cleanup.sh >> /home/youruser/cleanup.log 2>&1
Explanation & checks
  • Confirm PID with ps before issuing kill to avoid terminating the wrong process.
  • Try kill without -9 first to allow graceful cleanup.
  • Make scripts executable and use full paths inside them to run reliably under cron.
Reflection

After finishing, ask: did the log show the cleanup ran? If not, re-check the crontab syntax and script paths.

screens.title: Security and reliability considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Process management and scheduling are also operational security tasks. Monitoring processes can reveal unauthorized or unexpected activity, so regularly check running jobs for unknown PIDs or commands. When scheduling scripts, consider the permissions they run with; cron jobs run as the crontab owner, so a mistake in script content can expose data or escalate risk. Always validate scripts and avoid embedding secrets in plain text. For reliability, write idempotent scripts that can be safely run multiple times, and always redirect logs so failures are recorded. Use absolute paths and include environment setup at the top of scripts. Prefer system-level services for persistent daemons rather than ad-hoc background jobs tied to a user shell. Audit cron entries periodically and remove obsolete jobs. When terminating processes on shared systems, coordinate with other administrators to avoid disrupting critical services. These practices help you automate mundane maintenance without introducing security holes or causing unexpected downtime. Security and reliability considerations means validate and audit scheduled tasks, run scripts with least privilege, and log outputs to detect failures or unauthorized activity.. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Security & Reliability
Security guidelines
  • Run scheduled scripts with the least privilege necessary.
  • Do not store secrets in plain-text cron entries or scripts.
  • Audit crontab entries and remove unauthorized or obsolete jobs.
Reliability tip

Make scripts idempotent so reruns do not cause harm and log output for troubleshooting.

Operational checks
  • Periodically scan running processes for unexpected commands or users.
  • Confirm cron runs as expected by checking logs and crontab -l.
  • Prefer system services for long-running daemons rather than tying them to user shells.
Quick audit
List all user crontabs and review entries monthly. Remove or correct any entries that use insecure paths or elevated privileges without justification.

fullNarratorScript:
Processes are simply instances of running programs. In this lesson you will learn to observe what is running, make safe decisions when a process misbehaves, and automate routine maintenance so the system stays reliable. We'll use the core tools that administrators rely on: ps for snapshots, top and htop for live views, kill for signalling processes, nice and renice to tune priority, and cron and at to schedule recurring or one-time jobs. You will also see how parent and child process relationships matter when tracking PIDs, and why graceful termination is usually preferred over forceful kills. I'll show concrete commands you can run, highlight common mistakes—like relying on relative paths in cron—and give practical examples such as creating a daily cleanup script and scheduling it with crontab. By the end you'll understand not just the commands but why each tool matters for system responsiveness and predictable automation. Think about a time when a single runaway job slowed a server; these techniques are exactly what you would use to diagnose and fix it safely.

By the end of these screens you'll develop four core competencies. First, you'll be able to list running processes and interpret PID and PPID to trace parent-child relationships. This matters for debugging service trees and understanding which shell or service started a job. Second, you'll monitor live resource usage with top or htop and identify runaway processes by C P U or memory. That skill prevents system slowdown and helps prioritize fixes. Third, you'll safely control processes: use kill with SIGTERM first, then SIGKILL when necessary, and adjust priority with nice and renice so background work doesn't block interactive users. You'll practice when to prefer renice over killing. Fourth, you'll schedule recurring or one-off tasks with cron and at, learn crontab syntax, and avoid common pitfalls like relative paths or missing environment variables. Each objective includes a small verification milestone so you can confirm competency: list processes, kill a test job, renice a background task, and add a crontab entry that logs output to a file.

Practical verification keeps learning reliable. For each objective you'll perform a small, demonstrable task. For identifying processes, run a ps snapshot and read PID and PPID to show who started the job. For monitoring, start a harmless C P U work item in the background and confirm you can spot it in top or htop by PID and C P U percentage. For control, terminate that test job first with the default kill and, if needed, show how kill -9 removes it as a last resort. Then demonstrate adjusting a background job's priority with nice or renice so interactive workflows remain responsive. For scheduling, add a crontab entry that runs a simple script and redirects output to a log; confirm the job appears in crontab -l and writes to the log after the scheduled time. These checks focus on reproducible actions you can use in labs and in production to verify competency.

A process is simply an instance of a running program. Every process receives a unique process identifier, the PID, which the kernel uses to manage it. Processes often have parent-child relationships: the PPID field shows the parent's PID and reveals which process launched a child. For example, your interactive shell is typically the parent of commands you run. This parent-child relationship forms a process tree and matters for clean shutdowns and for understanding ownership and signal propagation. If a parent exits, the child may be adopted by the init process. In practical terms, when you want to trace why a background job is running, check PPID to find the originating shell or service. A common misconception is to treat PID as permanent; PIDs are reused over time, so relying on an old PID without re-checking can target the wrong process. To practice, use ps aux or ps -ef: ps aux shows user, PID, C P U and memory usage, and command, while ps -ef includes UID, PID, PPID, and a tree-like full format. Always re-check a PID immediately before sending signals. To reinforce this, try creating a short background job, note its PID, and then inspect its PPID to confirm the parent that launched it.

Real-time monitoring shows how resources are used now. top is available on nearly every Linux system and provides a continuously-updating snapshot of C P U, memory, tasks, and the processes consuming them. It sorts by C P U by default, so heavy compute jobs float to the top. htop is an enhanced alternative with color, easier navigation, and built-in shortcuts to kill processes or renice them. For troubleshooting, start top and watch the C P U column and load averages to judge system health. When you see a process consuming most C P U, note its PID and consider whether it should be limited, reniced, or terminated. A common mistake is to rely solely on instantaneous spikes; look for sustained high usage before deciding to kill a process. Also check memory usage and swap activity — high swap indicates memory pressure and can make a system sluggish. Practice: run a harmless C P U-heavy background job and watch it appear in top or htop, record its PID, then practice lowering its priority with renice or stopping it safely. These tools are about observation first and intervention second.

Signals are the mechanism by which the kernel or other processes communicate with a running process. The kill command sends a signal to a process identified by PID. The usual sequence is to request graceful termination with SIGTERM, which allows the program to catch the signal and clean up resources. If SIGTERM fails because the process is stuck or unresponsive, SIGKILL forces immediate termination and cannot be caught by the process. Use SIGKILL carefully, because it prevents cleanup and can leave temporary files or databases in an inconsistent state. Another useful signal is SIGHUP, which many daemons interpret as a request to reload their configuration without a full restart. Common tools include killall and pkill, which target processes by name or pattern; these are convenient but risk affecting multiple processes unexpectedly. A safe workflow is: locate PID with ps or top, run kill PID, check whether the process exits, and only then escalate to kill -9 PID if necessary. Always verify the process you are targeting is the one you intend, and consider service-specific management tools for daemons where available.

Job control is how you move commands between foreground and background and resume them when needed. When you append an ampersand to a command, the shell starts it in the background so you keep the prompt. Commands run in the foreground block the shell until they finish. You can suspend a foreground process and send it to the background, or bring background jobs back to the foreground. These controls matter during interactive sessions and for managing tasks without opening new terminals. A common misconception is that background jobs consume no resources; they still use C P U and memory but allow the shell to accept new input. In practice, start a safe C P U-intensive command in the background, note the job number or PID, use ps or top to monitor it, then use fg or kill if you need to interact with or stop it. Learning to manage jobs reduces the temptation to reboot or disrupt other users when a process blocks your terminal.

nice and renice change a process's scheduling priority, telling the kernel how politely that process should request C P U time. The nice value ranges from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). When you start a new process with nice, you set its initial niceness; renice changes niceness of an existing process by PID. For example, starting a long-running script with a positive nice value makes it yield C P U to interactive users, keeping the system responsive. Conversely, negative nice values increase priority and usually require administrative privileges.
